analysis.one_liner: Freezes imports of textiles, clothing, and shoes at roughly 1989 levels, growing only 1% a year.
analysis.headline: It never became law: after drawing 54 Senate cosponsors from both parties, its import quotas were folded into a spending bill that President George H.W. Bush vetoed, and the veto stood.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have capped imports of textiles, clothing, and nonrubber footwear at about their 1989 levels, allowing only 1% growth each year, and would have barred the President from negotiating any tariff cuts on those goods. It included carve-outs for Canada, Israel, U.S. territories, and Caribbean Basin countries, and a one-year pilot program to auction import licenses so quota rights were sold rather than handed out. Sponsors said it was needed to stop plant closings and job losses in U.S. textile and shoe factories. Everyone who buys clothes or shoes would have paid through higher prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic textile, apparel, and fiber manufacturers and domestic nonrubber footwear makers, concentrated in a handful of states, together with their workers. The bill's own findings describe 1.4 million textile, apparel, and fiber jobs lost since 1980 and a 45% drop in footwear employment since 1981, and the quotas were designed to halt that decline by freezing the growth of competing imports.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Textile, apparel, and footwear makers and workers

how_it_helps.text: Caps total 1990 imports of textiles and textile products at 101% of 1989 levels, with growth limited to 1% per year after that.
Freezes imports of nonrubber footwear at 1989 levels for 1990 and every year after, with a separate cap on high-priced footwear.
Prohibits the President from entering negotiations to lower tariffs on textiles, apparel, or footwear by any means, locking protection in against future trade deals.
The bill's findings cite a $26 billion textile trade deficit, 58% import penetration in clothing, and over 400 footwear factory closings since 1981 as the harm the quotas would stop.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, through higher prices on clothing and shoes as import supply is capped; importers and retailers, who would face auction costs for import licenses and less merchandise to sell; and foreign textile and footwear exporters, including low-wage countries in the Caribbean Basin whose allotments were capped.

drawbacks.text: A hard cap on import supply raises the price of imported clothing and shoes, and retailers pass that on; low-income households spend a larger share of their income on clothing, so a broad quota acts like a regressive sales tax on a basic necessity.

The bill itself acknowledges the quotas would breach existing trade agreements, requiring the President to grant offsetting concessions to trading partners — inviting retaliation against other U.S. exports.

It addresses import competition by shrinking the supply of goods rather than by helping displaced workers retrain or transition, leaving consumers to subsidize an industry already at 58% import penetration in apparel and 80% in footwear.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered real, immediate protection to a shrinking domestic industry and its remaining workers, and its license-auction pilot was an unusual effort to route quota rents to the Treasury instead of to license holders. But the standard economics of apparel and footwear quotas cut hard against it: the consumer cost per job preserved historically ran far above the wages of the jobs saved, and the burden fell on every household that buys clothes. It protected a concentrated domestic industry by spreading a large, largely invisible cost across all consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It never came up for a vote on its own; the Finance Committee folded its quota provisions into another bill in June 1990, that bill was vetoed by President Bush, and the Senate fell short of the two-thirds needed to override — so the quotas died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 4, 1990 by Sen. Hollings with 54 cosponsors, and read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
The Finance Committee held hearings on June 7, 1990.
On June 21, 1990, the committee ordered the measure incorporated into H.R. 4328 without amendment and without recommendation — meaning it was folded into another bill rather than advanced on its own.
The bill containing the textile quotas was vetoed by President George H.W. Bush in 1990, and the Senate override vote fell short of the two-thirds majority required, so the quotas never became law.
Congress ended January 3, 1991, with no Senate vote on S. 2411 itself.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Clothing and shoe buyers, plus importers and retailers, were better off because the bill died — they kept access to lower-priced imported goods. Foreign apparel exporters also kept their market access. The bill's intended beneficiaries, domestic textile and footwear producers, gained nothing and continued to lose ground to imports.

for.name: Sen. Ernest F. Hollings
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and wrote its findings and quota scheme to protect his state's textile industry.

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on June 7, 1990, then ordered the bill's provisions incorporated into H.R. 4328 without amendment and without recommendation.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill carrying the textile import quotas in 1990; the veto stood when the Senate override fell short of two-thirds.

against.name: Importers and retailers of apparel and footwear
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against mandatory textile and footwear quotas, which would cut their merchandise supply and raise their costs.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 36 of 55 Senate Democrats and 18 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored — but the veto came from a Republican president, and the decisive override fight split along party lines.

industries.note: A 1%-growth import cap would have protected their shrinking share of the U.S. market. Their gain would come directly out of clothing buyers' budgets in the form of higher prices.

Import levels would have been frozen at 1989 volumes indefinitely, halting an industry collapse that had seen 400-plus factory closings since 1981. The cost of that protection would fall on every shoe purchaser.
The bill's findings argue imports shifted demand to foreign cotton and wool, costing cotton growers over $1 billion a year; quotas would rebuild domestic demand for raw fiber.

Frozen import volumes and a mandatory license-auction pilot would reduce what they could sell and add auction costs. Their interest in plentiful cheap imports ran alongside consumers' interest in low prices.
The quotas capped their access to the U.S. market, hitting low-wage Caribbean Basin countries with fixed allotments. Their gain from open trade coincided with cheaper goods for U.S. consumers.
